L74: In the case that S is hyperbolic, its universal cover is the hyperbolic plane \({\mathbb {H}}^{2}\). The hyperbolic metric of \({\mathbb {H}}^{2}\) induces a complete Riemannian metric of constant negative curvature on S and it holds that its group \(\mathrm{Isom}^{+}(S)\) of orientation-preserving isometries coincides with \(\mathrm{Aut}(S)\).
L75: A dessin d’enfant (or just a dessin) is a pair \({\mathcal D}=(X,{\mathcal G})\), where X is a surface (either compact or not), \({\mathcal G} \subset X\) is a bipartite graph (vertices are either black or white and adjacent ones have different colors) where each vertex has finite degree and each connected component of \(X \smallsetminus {\mathcal G}\), called a face, is homeomorphic to an open disc and bounded by a finite set of edges (an edge might be internal to a face).
L76: Each dessin d’enfant on X induces a unique (up to biholomorphisms) Riemann surface structure on it [【30†5】, 【31†12】]. Dessins, on a compact surface X, were first introduced by Grothendieck in his Esquisse d’un Programme (1984) [【32†9】] (we call these dessins as Grothendieck’s dessins).
L77: In this case, such a Riemann surface structure can be described by an algebraic curve defined over the field of algebraic numbers \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\) and Grothendieck’s idea was to use such a combinatorial tool to obtain information on the structure of the absolute Galois group \(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb Q}/{\mathbb Q})\). Generalities on Grothendieck’s dessins can be found, for instance, in [【30†5】,【33†6】,【34†7】, 【32†9】, 【31†12】].
L78: The mapping class group associated to X is defined to be \(\mathrm{Map}(X)=\mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)/\mathrm{Hom}_{0}(X)\), where \(\mathrm{Hom}_{0}(X)\) is the subgroup of homeomorphisms which are isotopic to the identity. Let \(\theta :\mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X) \rightarrow \mathrm{Map}(X)\) denote the quotient group projection.
L79: The automorphisms of the bipartite graph \({\mathcal G}\), denoted by \(\mathrm{Aut}_{bip}({\mathcal G})\), is the group consisting of automorphisms of the graph that keep invariant black (respectively, white) vertices (called automorphisms of the bipartite graph).
L80: Let \(\widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathcal D})\) be the subgroup of \(\mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)\) consisting of those \(\phi \in \mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)\) keeping invariant \({\mathcal G}\) and inducing an element of \(\mathrm{Aut}_{bip}({\mathcal G})\). Note that, by performing any isotopy of \(\phi \in \widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathcal D})\) relative the vertices and keeping invariant the edges, we obtain the same automorphism of the bipartite graph; so this group is always uncountable.
L81: The group \(\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D}):=\theta (\widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathcal D}))\) is called the group of automorphisms of the dessin \({\mathcal D}\) (this permits us to talk about the topological action of this group on X).
L82: There is a natural injective homomorphism \(\rho :\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Aut}_{bip}({\mathcal G})\), so this provides a natural copy of \(\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D})\) inside \(\mathrm{Aut}_{bip}({\mathcal G})\) (i.e., we can see \(\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D})\) as those bipartite graph automorphisms of \({\mathcal G}\) that can be extended to an element of \(\mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)\)).
L83: As previously said, the dessin \({\mathcal D}\) induces a (unique up to biholomorphisms) Riemann surface structure S on X. In this case, there is a subgroup of \(\mathrm{Aut}(S)\) which is isomorphic (by \(\theta \)) to \(\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D})\), that is, we may see \(\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D}) \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)=\mathrm{Isom}^{+}(S)\). Now, as such a subgroup keeps invariant a non-empty discrete set of points (the black vertices), it is always a countable group.
L84: If \(\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D})\) acts transitively on the set of edges of the graph, then the dessin is called regular (in this case, \(\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D})\) is necessarily generated by two elements) [【30†5】, 【31†12】]. If X is compact, then \(\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D})\) is necessarily finite. If X is non-compact, then \(\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D})\) might be infinite (but countable).
L85: In [【35†10】, 【36†11】] it was observed that every finite group G is isomorphic to the group of automorphisms of some Grothendieck’s dessin (moreover, if G is generated by two elements, then the dessin can be chosen to be regular). In [【35†10】], it was also proved the existence for G infinite, but assuming it was finitely generated.
L86: Our first result is the following, which extends the above for any countable group. Moreover, we build a surface in which we realize any given group together with its subgroup lattice.
L87: ### Theorem 1

L1085@P23: 9 Dessins d’enfants
L1086@P23: 9.1 Main definitions
L1087@P23: Introduction and developments on the theory of dessins d’enfants can be
L1088@P23: found in [10] [11] [6] [15] [12] [7]. The definition of dessins may differ following
L1089@P23: the authors. For simplicity, we will use the following ”standard” one:
L1090@P23: Definition 6 [7] [15] [12] A dessin d’enfants (or simply a dessin) is a couple
L1091@P23: (X, D), where X is an (oriented) topological surface and D a finite bicolored
L1092@P23: graph on it such that X\D is a finite union of disjoint topological discs.
L1093@P23: Figure 4: A graph on a surface of genus 2
L1094@P23: As any finite graph, a dessin has a finite set of vertices V and a finite set of
L1095@P23: edges E. As a bicolored graph, each vertex can be colored in white or black,
L1096@P23: in such a way that the colors of two consecutive vertices on the same edge
L1097@P23: are different.
L1098@P23: The definition of a dessin by A. Grothendieck is a little bit more general :
L1099@P23: One simply considers a graph on a surface X such that X\D is a finite
L1100@P23: union of disjoint topological discs, without the bipartite property. However,
L1101@P23: one can recover the previous definition by coloring each vertex is black, and
L1102@P23: adding a white vertex in the interior of each edge. One gets a bipartite
L1103@P23: graph whose each white vertex has valence 2. The reader will check that
L1104@P23: many results of the following sections does not need a coloring of the dessin.
L1105@P23-24: 249.2 Triangulation associated to a dessin
L1106@P24: To each dessin (X, D) is associated a triangulation T built as follows :
L1107@P24: 1. In the interior of each face f of D, we choose a new vertex (marked
L1108@P24: by ∗ and called the center of f).
L1109@P24: 2. From each white (resp. black) vertex v of f, we draw a new edge joining
L1110@P24: v to ∗ so that the interior of two different edges have no intersection
L1111@P24: points, and the interior of such an edge has no intersection points with
L1112@P24: the edges of f. This process induces a triangulation of f. Remark
L1113@P24: however that two adjacent triangles may have two common edges.
L1114@P24: 3. By continuing this process for each face f of D, we get a triangulation
L1115@P24: of X. Since X is oriented, we can color any triangle in white and its
L1116@P24: adjacent ones in black, getting two classes of triangles of T , (of types
L1117@P24: + and type − for instance).
